dekalog-1989.gazette: Ten hour-long films, one Warsaw housing estate, made for Polish television at the end of the 1980s. Kieslowski keeps the music withheld and the camera at eye level, shooting stairwells and kitchens the way a documentary crew would find them — the same block, the same lifts, neighbours crossing between stories. The commandments are never named on screen; the address does the work.

do-the-right-thing-1989.gazette: The closing dedication names people killed in real incidents, among them Michael Stewart, who died after being taken into custody by New York transit police in 1983, and Michael Griffith, killed in Howard Beach in 1986. Radio Raheem dies the same way, held at the neck by an officer on a Bed-Stuy street while the block watches. Lee released it in the summer of 1989, two and a half years after Howard Beach.

the-hunt-for-red-october.gazette: The production had Navy cooperation and worked aboard real submarines, and the procedure shows: passive sonar, running silent, a hunt conducted entirely by ear. Argument in this film is technical — men reading a trace on a screen and disagreeing about what it means, with the ship's fate resting on the reading. Serving submariners have been checking it against their own training for decades.
the-hunt-for-red-october.prism: The accuracy is doing quiet argumentative work: if the machines and the drills are right, a Soviet captain deciding to walk away starts to feel like engineering rather than wish. That's the trade — it plays as a thriller about competence instead of a thriller about ideology.

to-live-1994.gazette: Fugui's household surrenders its iron to a backyard furnace, the campaign that had villages smelting pots and tools into unusable pig iron during the Great Leap Forward. The film carries one family from the 1940s through the famine years into the Cultural Revolution, marking each era by what the state asks them to hand over and who is missing afterward. Chinese authorities banned it.

braveheart-1995.gazette: William Wallace was real, Stirling Bridge was real, and the bridge is absent from the battle. Prima nocta, the lord's claim on a bride's wedding night, has no footing in Scottish law and belongs to the film rather than the record. Historians have been issuing corrections since 1995; the film has comfortably outrun them.

underground-1995.gazette: Kusturica's cellar holds a group of Belgraders who keep manufacturing weapons for a war that ended decades earlier, kept there by a friend who tells them the occupation continues. The film runs from the 1941 bombing of Belgrade through Tito's Yugoslavia to the wars that took it apart, splicing newsreel so its invented characters walk through documented history. It took the Palme d'Or in May 1995, with Sarajevo still under siege.
underground-1995.prism: The method — dropping fictional men into real footage so the seam disappears — is precisely what the film accuses the Titoist state of doing to its own citizens. The fight that followed was over whether you can indict propaganda while so visibly enjoying its tools.

peppermint-candy-2000.gazette: One chapter of Lee Chang-dong's backward chronology puts its protagonist in uniform in Gwangju in May 1980, during the suppression in which South Korean troops killed civilians. Because the film runs in reverse, the massacre arrives late, as the explanation for a man the audience has already watched fall apart. By 2000 the state had reclassified Gwangju from rebellion to democratic uprising and put the men who ordered the crackdown on trial.

vengeance-is-mine-1979.gazette: Imamura worked from Ryūzō Saki's reported account of Akira Nishiguchi, who killed a series of people in 1963 and stayed ahead of a nationwide manhunt for months on forged names and small confidence tricks. The film keeps the procedural bones — the swindles, the aliases, the arrest — and declines to supply the motive the case file never produced. Nishiguchi was executed in 1970.

pixote-1980.gazette: Babenco cast Fernando Ramos da Silva, a boy from the São Paulo periphery with no training, and filled the reformatory around him with children living the same life. The institutions are filmed as institutions: corridors, headcounts, night, the camera keeping its distance while the state processes minors it has otherwise abandoned. Da Silva was shot dead by police in 1987, at nineteen.
pixote-1980.prism: Casting real children gave the film its unfakeable texture and gave one of them a face the police could later recognise. The realism contract cuts both ways — it borrowed a life to make a claim about how such lives end, and then the claim proved itself.

raging-bull-1980.gazette: Scorsese built the film from LaMotta's 1970 memoir, with LaMotta himself training De Niro in the ring. It keeps the 1947 bout against Billy Fox that got him suspended on suspicion of taking a dive, and it keeps the marriages as he wrote them — which is to say from the vantage of the man throwing the punches. He ended up working nightclub rooms with a microphone.

the-elephant-man-1980.gazette: Joseph Merrick spent his last years in rooms at the London Hospital, taken in from 1886 under the surgeon Frederick Treves, whose memoir supplied most of what anyone knows about him. Lynch follows that account closely enough to inherit its mistakes, including the name — Treves wrote him down as John. Merrick died in 1890, aged twenty-seven, in his bed at the hospital.

chariots-of-fire-1981.gazette: Harold Abrahams and Eric Liddell both ran at the 1924 Paris Olympics and both won, Abrahams the 100 metres, Liddell the 400. The film has Liddell discover the Sunday heats aboard the boat to France; in fact he had known for months and trained for the longer distance accordingly. That compression is the picture's most scrutinised liberty, and it has been scrutinised at length.
chariots-of-fire-1981.prism: Moving the discovery onto the boat buys a scene of conscience under pressure and pays for it with the truer thing: a man who decided quietly, early, with time to prepare. Films need the choice to be visible. Character usually isn't.

sans-soleil-1983.gazette: Marker assembled the film from footage he shot himself — Tokyo, Iceland, Cape Verde, Guinea-Bissau — and set it behind letters from a cameraman who does not exist. The Guinea-Bissau passages follow Amílcar Cabral's liberation struggle through to the 1980 coup that removed his brother from the presidency, a revolution outliving the terms on which it was won. Everything in the frame happened; the voice explaining it never did.

amadeus-1984.gazette: Salieri and Mozart were both real, both in Vienna, and rivals in the ordinary court sense of competing for posts, pupils and commissions. The poisoning story comes from rumours circulating around Salieri's final illness in the 1820s, decades after Mozart died in 1791, and Shaffer built his play on that gossip with his eyes open. Musicologists have been objecting since 1984, while Salieri's own operas returned to the recording catalogue largely because of it.

taipei-story-1985.gazette: Yang shot Taipei while it was being rebuilt, with Hou Hsiao-hsien in the lead and the city playing itself: neon over demolition lots, office floors that had not existed a decade earlier. The camera holds still and holds long, letting scenes run past the point where a plot would cut away. What it records is a generation stranded between a family textile trade and a computer economy.
taipei-story-1985.prism: The long takes aren't patience for its own sake — that's how much time it takes to show two people who cannot name what has gone wrong between them. Cut faster and you get a breakup; hold, and you get an economy doing it to them.
